newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai PM refuses to back down on eve of debate.
newsitem.headline: Thai PM refuses to back down on eve of debate.

text.p: Thai prime minister Banharn Silpa-archa said in a newspaper interview published Tuesday that he would not resign and was ready to face the no-confidence motion tabled against him in parliament.

Banharn's 14-month-old, six-party coalition government has been sharply attacked by the opposition and the local media over its handling of the economy and domestic politics. Debate on the motion starts on Wednesday.
"I have said all along that I am not tied to the position (of prime minister). But this does not mean I will back down," Banharn told the Bangkok Post.
"I am prepared to answer all questions from the accusations that I interfered, mismanagement of personnel, to poor economic performance," he added.
Debate on the no-confidence motion tabled by the opposition could last for more than two days, political analysts said.
The motion accuses Banharn of incompetence and economic mismanagement, among other things. He has denied the charges.
Speculation had been rife that Banharn may quit, hand over the premiership to a more acceptable politician or even dissolve parliament before the debate.
But some analysts expect Banharn to win the debate with the support of his coalition, which controls 209 of the 391 seats in parliament.
Barharn also told the Post that if he won the vote he would revamp his economic team to address urgent economic concerns.

Thailand has seen an economic slowdown, and economists have predicted the country's gross domestic product growth could fall below 7.0 percent this year from 8.6 percent in 1995. Export growth this year has also been sluggish compared with 1995.
"Let me say this. If I pass through this (debate), there will be definite change in the economic sphere, especially a new economic team," he said.

Banharn said recent declines in the Thai stock market were precipitated by his foes, whom he accused of dumping shares to force the market down and discredit him ahead of the debate. The Thai bourse has been near three-year-lows since early September.
"My sources at the stock market inform me that there are some groups dumping shares in an attempt to batter the market to tarnish my government's image," he said.
He blasted critics who said the talk that he might resign could be the reason for the recovery in the bourse since Friday.
"Do they know the real reason? It is because that (stock market) support funds went into place since last Friday. As long as foreigners withdraw funds, any market will go," he said.
An informal poll published on Tuesday by the Bangkok Post showed investors in Thailand believe a change in the country's political leadership would boost the stock market.

The poll showed more than half the 122 Thais surveyed thought the Stock Exchange of Thailand (SET) index would rise sharply over the next six months if there was a leadership change. Nearly 35 percent of the 29 foreign investors polled agreed, while 48 percent said the SET would rise slightly.
When asked about reports that Defence Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh might be preparing himself to be the next prime minister, Banharn said he would ignore such news.
Chavalit, who heads the second biggest party in the coalition, the New Aspiration Party, has said he would like to become premier in the future, but only through fresh elections.
